question: A previously healthy 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother after she noticed multiple painless, nonpruritic papules on her abdomen. The child attends daycare three times per week, and this past week one child was reported to have similar lesions. Her immunizations are up-to-date. Her brother had chickenpox one month ago. She is at the 50th percentile for height and the 60th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows several skin-colored, nontender, pearly papules with central umbilication on the abdomen and extremities. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Exposure to child with similar lesions -> Painless, nonpruritic papules on abdomen -> Skin-colored, pearly papules with central umbilication on abdomen and extremities -> Molluscum contagiosum -> 95%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 2-year-old girl with painless, nonpruritic papules on her abdomen and extremities is molluscum contagiosum, supported by exposure to a child with similar lesions and the presence of skin-colored, pearly papules with central umbilication. The evidence path confirming the location of molluscum contagiosum further strengthens this diagnosis.
analysis: The core medical principle guiding this case is the recognition of characteristic features of skin lesions and the importance of history in making a diagnosis. The presentation of painless, nonpruritic papules with central umbilication in a child attending daycare, with exposure to a similar case, strongly suggests molluscum contagiosum. The absence of systemic symptoms and the typical appearance of the lesions support this diagnosis.
